messages.author: 471d1a1624ff6440
messages.subject: 3-level hierarchical model
parts:
Hi,

I am wondering if anyone could show me how to code up the following model in INLA.

I have several observation data sets (positive, indexed in 2d-space and time) that are informative for the same underlying spatio-temporal process Z. I want to infer Z.

The observations are modelled in terms of Z hierarchically, with 2 intermediate latent levels, as follows

O_ij(s,t) ~ F(Y_ij(s,t))   
Y_ij = B_ij * M_i + E_ij
M_i = A_i * Z + E_i
Z ~ N(0, Q)

F(x) is some distribution with positive support and expectation depending on x through a suitable link function (say, Gamma with mean e^x). All observations O_ij(s,t) are conditionally independent. Each Y_ij, M_i and Z are spatio-temporal processes modelled as GMRFs (say, CAR in space and RW2 in time) with individual hyperparameters. All matrices B_ij and A_i are assumed to be known. The residuals E_ij and E_i are mutually independent Normal vectors with non-zero means and diagonal covariance (although the possibility to extend the E's to have spatio-temporal structure would be good). The data frame has columns (O,i,j,s,t). If anyone can help me this would be great, do let me know if I left out any crucial information. All Z,M,Y live on the same spatial and temporal support. The A and B matrices would typically be incidence matrices, picking out only a few elements of M and Z.

Also I'm trying to get an idea about what problem sizes are feasible. The numbers of i's and j's I have isn't too large, something like i=1,2,3 and j=1...5 for each i. In space and time there is lots of data, something like 150k points in space and 10k in time, so Z has dimension of order 10^9. Is that doable for INLA? If not, how much would I have to reduce the dimensionality of the problem?

Thanks!

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] 3-level hierarchical model
parts:
10^9 is in any case to large...

since you have so many data, but the latent is small, can you compute
things directly? Like starting with the joint prior for M, Z, and then
add the data, and simply use a Gaussian approximation of that?

In that case, you can do 10^9.

Yes, Z is a spatio-temporal process.
Each M_i is a known affine transformation of the process Z, plus structured and unstructured noise E_i.
Each Y_ij is a known affine transformation of the process M_i, plus structured and unstructured noise E_ij.
I want to infer the latent Z from the various observed spatio-temporal data sets Y_ij.
Does that help?
